english: I'd like to open an account
usage: I'd like to open an account
Polite, the everyday line at the bank counter
I'm here to open an account
개설하다 is the formal/bank-form word for 'open (an account)'
I came to open a bankbook
통장 (passbook) is what people say casually for a basic account
I'm looking to open an account
-는데요 softens it and invites the teller to guide you
examples: 계좌 만들고 싶어요.
I'd like to open an account.
Said to the teller as you sit down; simplest opener
외국인인데 계좌 만들 수 있어요?
I'm a foreigner — can I open an account?
외국인인데 flags your status so they tell you what documents you need
월급 받을 계좌 하나 개설하려고 왔는데요.
I came to open an account to receive my salary.
Give the purpose (월급 받을, 'to receive salary'); banks ask why
nuance: 계좌 만들고 싶어요 is 계좌 (Sino-Korean 計座, 'account') + 만들다 ('to make') + -고 싶어요 ('want to'), the plain spoken way to tell a teller you want to open an account. Two words matter here: 계좌 is the technical 'account' (a number, used on forms and apps), while 통장 literally means the physical 'bankbook/passbook' but in daily speech doubles as 'account' — so 통장 만들고 싶어요 sounds just as natural and a bit more colloquial. The bank's own paperwork and staff prefer the verb 개설하다 ('to establish/open'), so you'll hear 계좌 개설; you can mirror it with 개설하려고요 to sound on-register. The English-speaker trap is translating 'open' literally as 열다 ('to open a door/lid') and saying 계좌 열고 싶어요 — that is wrong; an account is 만들다 ('make') or 개설하다, never 열다. Default to 만들고 싶어요 with any teller; there is no 반말 version you'd use here since it's always a staff setting.

english: I'd like to check my balance
usage: I'd like to check my balance
Polite, said to a teller or about an ATM
조회 ('inquiry/lookup') is the button word on ATMs and apps
How much is in my account?
잔고 is the casual everyday synonym for 'balance'
남다 ('to remain') framing, very natural in speech
examples: 잔액 확인하고 싶어요.
I'd like to check my balance.
Said to a teller, or to yourself before using the ATM
잔액 조회는 어디서 해요?
Where do I check the balance?
조회 is the exact menu word you'll tap on the ATM screen
이체하기 전에 잔액부터 확인할게요.
Before transferring, let me check the balance first.
잔액부터 ('balance first') — 부터 means 'starting with'
nuance: 잔액 확인하고 싶어요 is 잔액 (殘額, 'remaining amount = balance') + 확인하다 ('to check/confirm') + -고 싶어요. There are two near-synonyms you must keep straight: 잔액 is the formal term printed on receipts, ATM menus, and statements, while 잔고 ('balance / what's left') is the warmer everyday word people use when chatting ('통장에 잔고가 없어' = 'my account's empty'). On machines and in apps the action is labeled 잔액 조회 ('balance inquiry'), where 조회 specifically means looking up information, so 조회 is the verb you tap, and 확인 is the broader 'check/confirm' you say aloud. The English-speaker trap is reaching for 균형 — the dictionary gives 균형 for 'balance', but 균형 means equilibrium/physical balance (as in keeping your balance), NEVER a bank balance. Saying 통장 균형 confuses Koreans completely. Also note the particle: it's 잔액을 확인하다 (object), so don't say 잔액에 확인하다. To a teller use the polite form; with a friend you'd casually ask 잔고 얼마야?.

english: I'm going to withdraw some cash
usage: I'm going to take out some cash
Casual-polite; 뽑다 ('pull out') is the everyday verb for ATM cash
I'd like to make a withdrawal
출금 (出金) is the formal/screen word for 'withdrawal'
I'm going to withdraw some money
찾다 (lit. 'find/retrieve') is the standard verb for getting your money out
Stating the amount; 만 ('only') limits it
examples: 현금 좀 뽑으려고요.
I'm going to take out some cash.
Said heading to the ATM, or to a teller for over-the-counter cash
여기 ATM에서 출금돼요?
Can I withdraw at this ATM?
출금되다 ('withdrawal is possible') checks if your card works here
통장에서 십만 원 찾고 싶은데요.
I'd like to withdraw 100,000 won from my account.
통장에서 ('from the account') + 찾다 — the from-source takes 에서
nuance: 현금 좀 뽑으려고요 is 현금 ('cash', 現金) + 좀 (softener) + 뽑다 ('to pull/draw out') + -으려고요 ('I intend to'). Korean has three overlapping verbs for getting money out, and choosing right is the whole game: 뽑다 ('pull out') is the breezy spoken verb specifically for pulling cash from an ATM (돈 뽑다 = 'hit the ATM'); 찾다 — which elsewhere means 'find' — is the neutral standard 'withdraw' (돈을 찾다) used in any context, counter or machine; and 출금하다 (出金) is the formal Sino-Korean word you see on screens and forms. The opposite, depositing, is 입금하다 / 넣다 — keep 출금 (out) vs 입금 (in) firmly apart, since swapping them at a teller causes real mistakes. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'withdraw' as 철수하다 (which is 'withdraw troops/retreat!') or 인출 used as a bare verb; say 뽑다 or 찾다 in speech. Another trap: 찾다 here does NOT mean 'look for' — 돈 찾으러 가요 means 'going to withdraw money', not 'going to look for money'. With friends drop to 돈 좀 뽑을게.

Those mean military/strategic withdrawal (retreat). For money it's 출금하다 / 돈을 찾다 / 돈을 뽑다.

In a banking context 찾다 means 'withdraw' (retrieve your money), not 'search'. 돈 찾으러 왔어요 = 'I came to withdraw money'.

usage: Polite-neutral; the basic question before any transaction
When you already expect a fee and want the amount
붙다 ('to be attached') is how Koreans say a fee is 'added on'
면제되다 ('to be exempted') — asking if you qualify for free
examples: 수수료 있어요?
Is there a fee?
Asked before transferring or withdrawing at another bank's ATM
다른 은행 ATM이라 수수료 붙어요?
It's another bank's ATM — will a fee be charged?
다른 은행 ATM ('other bank's ATM') is exactly when fees apply
이체 수수료는 면제고, 출금만 수수료 있어요.
Transfer fees are waived; only withdrawals have a fee.
Hear the teller distinguish 이체 vs 출금 fees
nuance: 수수료 있어요? is 수수료 (手數料, 'handling fee/commission') + 있어요? ('is there?'). 수수료 is the all-purpose word for a transaction fee — ATM fees, transfer fees, wire fees, exchange margins — so it's the single most useful money word at a Korean bank. The natural verb pairing is 붙다 ('to stick/be attached'): Koreans say 수수료가 붙어요 ('a fee gets tacked on'), which sounds more idiomatic than the textbook 수수료를 내다 ('to pay a fee'); both are correct but 붙다 is what you'll hear about charges appearing automatically. To ask about getting out of a fee, use 면제 ('exemption'): 수수료 면제돼요?. The dividing line from 요금 is scope: 요금 is a 'charge/fare' for a service or utility (전기 요금, 'electricity bill'; 택시 요금, 'taxi fare'), while 수수료 is specifically the bank's cut for handling a transaction — don't ask a bank about 요금. The English-speaker trap is saying 비용 ('cost/expense') or 가격 ('price'), which are too generic and sound off for a banking fee. With staff keep 있어요?; the structure stays the same in casual speech (수수료 있어?).

붙다 ('to be attached') is intransitive — the fee attaches itself: 수수료가 붙어요 (subject 가). With an object particle it'd be the transitive 붙이다. Use 수수료가 붙어요.

usage: What the teller/machine tells YOU; 입력하다 = 'input'
눌러 주세요 ('please press') — common spoken version at a counter
자리 = 'digit'; Korean card PINs are usually 네 자리 (4 digits)
What YOU say when you can't remember it
examples: 비밀번호 입력해 주세요.
Please enter your PIN.
The teller says this, pushing the keypad toward you
비밀번호 네 자리 눌러 주세요.
Please key in your 4-digit PIN.
네 자리 specifies four digits, the standard for cards
비밀번호 세 번 틀려서 카드가 잠겼어요.
I got the PIN wrong 3 times so my card got locked.
세 번 틀리다 ('wrong 3 times') is the usual lockout trigger
nuance: 비밀번호 (秘密番號, lit. 'secret number') is the one word covering PIN, password, and door code — Korean does NOT split 'PIN' from 'password' the way English does, so use 비밀번호 for your card PIN, your app login, and the restroom door code alike. With it you'll hear two verbs: 입력하다 ('to input', the formal screen word) and 누르다 ('to press', the spoken 'key it in') — 비밀번호 입력해 주세요 vs 비밀번호 눌러 주세요 are interchangeable, the latter just warmer. Note this phrase is usually said TO you by staff or the machine (the honorific 주세요 makes it a polite request to the customer); when YOU forgot it, you flip to 비밀번호 잊어버렸어요. Counting digits uses 자리 ('place/digit'): 네 자리 = four digits. The English-speaker trap is calling it 패스워드 (the loanword exists but sounds tech-only/IT) when 비밀번호 is the universal term, or saying 암호 — which means 'cipher/passcode' and feels more like a secret code or encryption than your everyday bank PIN. Also don't confuse 비밀번호 with 계좌번호 (account number) — one is secret, one you freely give out.

english: I'd like to send money here
usage: I'd like to send money here
Polite; 송금 (送金) is the formal word for 'remittance'; 여기로 marks the destination
I want to send money to this account
보내다 ('to send') is the plain everyday verb
I'd like to do a bank transfer
해외 송금 = international remittance; ask if it's possible
examples: 여기로 송금하고 싶어요.
I'd like to send money here.
Handing over the account details to the teller
이 계좌로 삼십만 원 보내 주세요.
Please send 300,000 won to this account.
이 계좌로 ('to this account') — destination takes the particle 로/으로
미국에 있는 가족한테 송금하려고 하는데요.
I'm trying to send money to family in the US.
가족한테 ('to family') — to a PERSON use 한테; 미국에 marks the place
nuance: 여기 송금하고 싶어요 uses 송금 (送金, lit. 'send-money', i.e. 'remittance') + 하다 + -고 싶어요. Three terms cluster here and the distinctions are practical: 송금 is the formal umbrella for sending money to someone (especially the word for overseas/wire transfers, 해외 송금); 계좌이체 (or just 이체) specifically means an account-to-account electronic transfer you do in an app or ATM; and 보내다 ('to send') is the plain verbal way to say it (돈 보내다). For a teller, 송금하고 싶어요 or 이체하고 싶어요 both work. The make-or-break point is particles for the destination: an account/bank/place takes 로/으로 ('to') — 이 계좌로 보내다 — while a PERSON takes 한테 / 에게 — 친구한테 송금하다. English speakers routinely overuse 에 here (이 계좌에 보내다 sounds off; native is 이 계좌로). Another trap is confusing 송금 (sending OUT) with 입금 (money coming IN to an account); if you want someone to pay YOU, you give them your 계좌번호 and they 입금/송금 to you. Don't translate 'transfer' as 옮기다 ('to move/relocate an object') — money transfer is 이체 / 송금, never 옮기다.

Money goes TO an account with 로/으로: 이 계좌로 보내 주세요. 이 계좌에 보내다 sounds unnatural to natives.
Using 한테/에게 for an account number.

usage: Polite; announcing you'll do an account transfer
Choosing transfer as the payment method (vs card/cash)
I've made the transfer / I sent it
Past tense — telling someone the money's been sent
I'll transfer it to you right away
-아/어 드리다 (humble favor) when sending to someone you respect
examples: 이체할게요.
I'll make the transfer.
Said at the counter or aloud as you do it in the app
현금 없어서 계좌이체로 할게요.
I have no cash, so I'll pay by transfer.
계좌이체로 ('by transfer') as the payment method
방금 이체했는데 입금됐는지 확인 좀 해 주세요.
I just transferred it — please check if it arrived.

한도 is 限度, 'limit/ceiling'.

Vocabulary: 한도 ('limit/quota/ceiling') is specifically a permitted maximum, not to be confused with 한계 ('limit' in the sense of a boundary of ability/endurance, e.g. 체력의 한계) — you say 이체 한도, never 이체 한계. Another is the verb: an account limit is 올리다/높이다 ('raise'), not 늘리다 in the sense of physically multiplying — though 한도를 늘리다 ('increase the limit') is also acceptable.

mistakes: Using 한계 instead of 한도 for an account cap.
한도 (限度) is a permitted maximum/quota (이체 한도). 한계 is a limit of ability/endurance (체력의 한계). For a transfer or withdrawal cap, always 한도.
Confusing 한도 (cap) with 잔액 (balance).
한도 is the MAX you're allowed to move; 잔액 is how much money you actually have. You can be blocked by a low 한도 even with a high 잔액. They're different problems.
Saying 한도 크게 해 주세요.
The idiomatic verb for a cap is 올리다/높이다 ('raise'): 한도 좀 올려 주세요. 크게 하다 ('make it big') sounds off for a numeric limit.
